title: Lattice Lindbladian simulation by patching and merging
abstract: Simulating the dynamics of dissipative quantum many-body systems governed by local Lindbladians is a fundamental task in quantum computation. While the near-optimal gate count has been achieved for Hamiltonian simulation, comparable results for Lindbladian simulation remain elusive. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for lattice Lindbladians by exploiting their locality. First, we consider sparsely dissipative systems, in which the dissipation is sparsely located, including boundary-driven systems. We establish a near-optimal quantum algorithm for their dynamics with gate count $O(Nt \, \mathrm{polylog}(Nt/\varepsilon))$, where $N$ is the system size, $t$ is the evolution time, and $\varepsilon$ is the allowable error. We then consider generic lattice Lindbladians with finite-range interactions and dissipation, and develop an algorithm for simulating time-evolved observables with gate count $O((Nt)^{4/3} \, \mathrm{polylog}(Nt/\varepsilon))$ per sample with the sampling complexity $Θ(\varepsilon^{-2})$. The gate count has the smallest known dependence on the system size among algorithms retaining polylogarithmic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$. Our algorithms are based on two techniques that exploit locality: patching and merging. Patching decomposes dissipative dynamics into dynamics on subsystems with exponentially small error, generalizing a key idea underlying the Haah-Hastings-Kothari-Low algorithm for near-optimal Hamiltonian simulation. Merging absorbs reversed dissipative dynamics into other parts of the evolution, substantially reducing the overhead associated with quasi-probabilistic sampling. These results demonstrate that locality can be fully exploited to achieve fast quantum simulation of dissipative many-body dynamics, opening the way to applications such as predicting nonequilibrium phenomena and preparing desirable quantum states.
summary: This paper presents quantum algorithms to simulate the dynamics of dissipative quantum many-body systems described by Lindbladians. By exploiting the locality of the dissipation using novel 'patching' and 'merging' techniques, the authors achieve near-optimal gate counts for sparsely dissipative systems. This advances the field by providing scalable quantum tools for simulating open quantum dynamics.
main_problem: The core problem is developing quantum algorithms to simulate the time evolution of dissipative quantum many-body systems governed by local Lindbladians.
main_result: The authors establish near-optimal quantum algorithms for sparsely dissipative systems, achieving a gate count of O(Nt polylog(Nt/epsilon)), and present an algorithm for generic systems with a scaling of O((Nt)^(4/3) polylog(Nt/epsilon)).
method: The algorithms exploit locality using two key techniques: 'patching' to decompose dynamics into subsystems and 'merging' to absorb reversed dissipative dynamics, generalizing ideas from Hamiltonian simulation.
model_or_system: The system is a lattice ($\Lambda$) described by the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equation, $ rac{d}{dt}ho(t) = Lho(t)$, where $L$ is the local Lindbladian.
key_observables: Gate Count (primary efficiency metric), time-evolved state $ho(t)$, and time-evolved observables $\langle Oangleho(t)$.
important_parameters: System size ($N$), evolution time ($t$), and allowable error ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on the locality of the Lindbladians and the ability to decompose the evolution using patching and merging techniques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decomposition of the lattice into internal and external boundaries for high-dimensional systems, detailing the iterative steps of the patching and merging protocol.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the problem (Lindbladian simulation), then introducing the locality-exploiting techniques (patching/merging), and finally presenting the main theorems for sparsely dissipative and generic lattice Lindbladians, culminating in complexity analysis.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the simulation of open quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding decoherence and non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum computation and quantum simulation.
